# `TLDR` 

This is a blog post that summarizes the things I found helpful while going through the various mathematical notation systems and `R` syntax for multilevel models^[otherwise known as hierarchical models, mixed models, panel data models, etc.] 

# Linear models and `lm`

We will first start with the **linear models**, where we don't consider the effects of any grouping variable. We will first use the `trees` data set:  

```{r}
#| layout-ncol: 2

trees %>% ggplot(aes(x = Height, y = Volume)) + 
  geom_point()

trees %>% ggplot(aes(x = Girth, y = Volume, color = Height)) + 
  geom_point()

# trees %>% ggplot(aes(x = log(Girth), y = log(Volume), color = log(Height))) + 
#   geom_point()
```

From the above plot, there seems to be a linear relationship between `Volumne` and `Girth`. We can try to fit a linear model using the `lm` function: 

```{r}
m1 <- lm(Volume ~ Height + Girth, data = trees)
m1
```

:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
In general, we can specify linear models via the **matrix notation** as follows: 

$$\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{X}\mathbf{\beta} + \mathbf{e}$$ where $\mathbf{y}$ is the response vector of length $n$, $\mathbf{X}$ is the *design matrix* of size $n \times p$, $\mathbf{\beta}$ is the $p$-vector and $\mathbf{e}$ is the error variable. 

We can also use the [`equatiomatic` package](https://datalorax.github.io/equatiomatic/) to turn `R` fomulae into latex equations: 

```{r}
extract_eq(m1)
```

:::

@tanakaSymbolicFormulaeLinear2019 provides a nice graph that connects the dots between the symbolic formulae used in `lm` and its connection to the mathematical equation. 

# Mixed models and `lmer` 

Often times we encounter data with some "grouping" factors, e.g., students' scores from schools from different districts, etc. Here we will use the data set used by [this chapter by Stef van Buuren in *Flexible Imputation of Missing Data*](https://stefvanbuuren.name/fimd/sec-threeformulations.html). This is data on school performance of grade 8 pupils in Dutch schools. There data were collected by Brandsma and Knuver (1989) and were used as the primary examples in Chapters 4 and 5 of Snijders and Bosker (2012). The data contains a mix of both pupil-level measuremetns and school-level measurements. 

```{r}
#| code-fold: true

data("brandsma", package = "mice")
df <- brandsma %>% select(sch, lpo, sex, den)

# there is NA data so we filter those out 
df <- df %>% na.omit() %>% 
# turn the other columns into factors 
  mutate(sch = as.factor(sch), 
         sex = as.factor(sex), 
         den = as.factor(den))

# df %>% glimpse()
# df %>% summary()
```

So according to this source^[https://stefvanbuuren.name/fimd/sec-threeformulations.html] there are three notational systems: 
1. level notation 
2. composite notation 
3. matrix notation 

... which is consistent with what I'm seeing in this other paper. 



## Level Notation 

- Introduced by Bryk and Raudenbush 1992 
- formulate a multilevel model as a **system of two equations**, one at level-1, and two at level-2: 
(Here I am substituting all the $c$s with all the $j$s in the original system)
$$\begin{align}
\texttt{lpo}_{ij} &= \beta_{0j} + \beta_{1j}\texttt{sex}_{ij} + \epsilon_{ij} \\ 
\beta_{0j} &= \gamma_{00} + \gamma_{01} \texttt{den}_j + u_{0j} \\ 
\beta_{1j} &= \gamma_{10} 
\end{align}
$$

where $\texttt{lpo}_{ij}$ is the test score of pupile $i$ in school $j$. 
Note here that the subscripts distinguish the level-1 and level-2 variables. 

## Composite Notation 

We can also substitute the level-2 models into level-1 model and result in the following single predictive equation: 

$$
\texttt{lpo}_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{sex}_{ij} + \beta_2 \texttt{den}_j + u_{0j} + \epsilon_{ij} 
$$

```{r}
m1 <- lmer(lpo ~ 1 + sex + den + (1 | sch), data = df)
m1
```

We can also use the equatiomatic package to double check: 

```{r}
extract_eq(m1)
```

And the version with the actual coefficient: 

```{r}
extract_eq(m1, use_coefs = TRUE)
```


## Matrix Notation 

Still the same model can be written in matrix notation as 

$$
y_j = X_j \beta + Z_j u_j + \epsilon_j
$$

where $y_j = \texttt{lpo}_j$ is a column vector containing the scores in cluster $j$, where $X_j = (1, \texttt{den}_j, \texttt{sec}_j)$ is the design matrix, a

## Domains and preferences 

- The matrix model formulation is favoured among statisticians^[for example, [this blog posts](https://stats.oarc.ucla.edu/other/mult-pkg/introduction-to-linear-mixed-models/) uses the matrix notation] 
- The level notation is common in the social sciences, as they separate the roles of level-1 and level-2 variables, which eases interpretation of the model and error structures 
- The composite formulation covers the middle ground, for its balance between compactness and clarity, and is used by the introductions into the multilevel analysis for applied researchers 
  - I think the Bayesian wind is most similar to this 

---

## Which of these map best to `lme4` and `brms` syntax? 

The composite notation maps best to `lme4` and `brms` syntax. 

What about the syntax? Xiaoying provides some lead here but it's like Wilkinson-Rogers -> Wilkinson-Rogers-Pinheiro-Bates (`lm(y ~ x + z)`) and then Paurl Burkner for the brms syntax (`response | aterms ~ pterms + (gterms | group)`). 


:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
## What's up with all this terminology? 

My mental model of how hierarchical models work is heavily influenced by @mcelreath2020statistical. In his book, McElreath said: 

> I adopt the terminology of @gelman2005analysis, who argues that the common term *random effects* hardly aids with understanding, for most people. Indeed, it seems to encourage misunderstanding, partly because the terms *fixed* and *random effects* mean different things to different statisticians. See pages 20--21 of Gelman's paper. I fully realize, however, that by trying to spread Gelman's alternative jargon, I am essentially splitting into a very strong wind.

The TLDR is that there have been a lot of different definitions of fixed and random effects in different contexts, across different disciplines. Gelman chose to sidestep the overloaded terms and define 

> ... effects (or coefficients) in a multilevel model as *constant* if they are identical for all groups in a population and *varying* if they are allowed to differ from group to group. 

What this implies in terms of how the math notation^[Referring to section 12.1 Notation from @gelman2007data] is that

- Units $i = 1, ..., n$ 
- Outcome measurements $y = (y_1, ..., y_n)$ 
- Regression predictors represented by an $n \times k$ matrix $X$ 
- Groups $j = 1, ..., J$. This works for a single level of grouping (e.g., students within schools, persons within states, tadpoles within tanks)
  - Occasioally use $k = 1, ..., K$ for a second level of grouping (e.g., students within schools within districts)
- Index variable $j[i]$ code group membership. For example, if you get $j[35] = 4$ that means the 35th data unit in the data belongs to group 4. 

:::

# Notation type 

1. Composite --- "composite form" see Singer 1998
  - "essentially the presentation used for mixed effects models" 
  - $\beta$ represent the average effects of variables that are known as *fixed effects*  
  - $u$ represents heterogeneity between the groups, typically called *random effects*  
  - closer in structure to the syntax used in SAS, STATA, and R (`nlme`, `lmer`) 
2. Level
  - Bayesian models "naturally related terms through hierarchical structures" 
3. Matrix 
  - the best way to express something succinctly 
  - $\mathbf{y} = X \mathbf{\beta} + Z \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{\epsilon}$ 
  - ... where $X_j$ is the **design matrix** for the fixed effects and $Z_j$ is the design matrix for the **random effects**.  

## Math notation and design formula 

According to @mcelreath2020statistical, it is a compact form of notation, that are intimately related to a "common matrix algebra description of linear models". If you've run `lmer` code before you know what something like `y ~ 1 + x` means. 

[Xiaoying Pu](https://xiaoyingpu.github.io/) provided a [cheat sheet](https://xiaoyingpu.github.io/note/cheat/) for reading/writing R formulas used in `lmer` and `brms`. 

In @barrRandomEffectsStructure2013, the provide a nice table. 

In @gaSoftwareFittingMultilevel2013, they looked at the software for fitting multilevel models, and they had a nice table^[Table 26.1] about statistical software packages containing modules/functions designed to fix various classes of mixed-effects models. Below I will reproduce this table, but focusing only on the `R` side of things: 

| `R` package | Linear Mixed Models <br> **LMM** | Generalized Linear Mixed Models <br> **GLMM** | Nonlinear Mixed Models <br> **NLMM** |
|---------|:-----|------:|:------:|
| [`nlme`](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/nlme/index.html)      | 12   |    12 |   12   |
| [`lme4`](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/lme4/index.html)     | 123  |   123 |  123   |
| [`brms`](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/brms/index.html)       | 1    |     1 |   1    |

: `R` software packages and functions for fitting mixed models.

We will leverage this paper^[Multilevel Model Notation - Establishing the commonalities] but use the dataset (`brandsma` object in the `mice` package) mentioned by this source^[https://stefvanbuuren.name/fimd/sec-threeformulations.html]. 

We will concentrate on four variables: 

- `sch`: school number 
- `lpo`: language test post, outcome at pupil level.
- `sex`: sex of pupil 
- `den`: school denomination, predictor at school level. 

## Some preliminary checks 

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| layout-ncol: 2

df %>% ggplot(aes(x = lpo, color = sex)) + 
  geom_density()

df %>% ggplot(aes(x = lpo, color = den)) + 
  geom_density() + 
  facet_wrap(~sex)
```


## Unconditional Means model 

$$y_{ij} = \beta_0 + u_{0j} + \epsilon_{ij}$$

The model posits that the score of a randomly selected student $i$ in a randomly selected school $j$ can be represented as a sum of: 

- the population mean $\beta_0$ 
- the effect of being in school $j$: $u_{0j}$
- the effect of being a particular student in school $j$: $\epsilon_{ij}$

## Composite Notation 

The same model can be rewritten as 
$$\texttt{lpo}_{ic}=\beta_0 + \beta_1 \texttt{sex}_{ic} + \beta_2 \texttt{den}_c + u_{0c} + \epsilon_{ic}$$
Which in Gelman notation, is something like (`TODO` this is not right ...)
$$\texttt{lpo}_{i} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \texttt{sex}_{\texttt{class}[i]} + \beta_2 \texttt{den}_{j[i]} + u_{0c} + \epsilon_{ic} $$

```{r}
# lmer(lpo ~ 1 + sex + den + (1 | 1 + sex + den), data = df)
```
